motion: This House believes that the internet must be subject to far stronger government regulation and platform accountability in order to protect society from misinformation, addiction, polarisation and exploitation, even at the cost of reduced openness and slower innovation.

vocab.definition: The systemic spread of false, misleading or manipulated content that undermines shared understanding of reality.
vocab.example: Unchecked information disorder has eroded public trust in elections, science and basic institutions.

vocab.definition: The deliberate design of platforms to maximise the time and emotional engagement users spend on them, often at the expense of well-being.
vocab.example: Infinite scroll and notification systems are tools of attention extraction engineered for profit.

vocab.definition: The automated boosting of content that generates strong reactions, frequently prioritising outrage and extremity over accuracy.
vocab.example: Algorithmic amplification turns fringe claims into mainstream controversies within hours.

vocab.definition: Compulsive, harmful overuse of online platforms that interferes with sleep, relationships, work and mental health.

vocab.definition: A system that systematically drives users toward more extreme and mutually hostile viewpoints.
vocab.example: Recommendation algorithms have functioned as a polarisation engine in multiple democracies.

vocab.definition: An economic model that harvests personal data on a massive scale to predict and influence behaviour for profit.
vocab.example: Surveillance capitalism treats human experience as a free raw material for corporate extraction.

vocab.definition: Legal or practical protection that allows large online services to avoid responsibility for the harms their systems enable.
vocab.example: Broad platform immunity has left victims of online abuse and misinformation with little recourse.

vocab.definition: The mental exhaustion and reduced critical capacity caused by continuous exposure to high volumes of competing claims and stimuli.
vocab.example: Constant cognitive overload leaves citizens less able to evaluate evidence or sustain complex debate.

vocab.definition: Coordinated campaigns of abuse, threats or reputational destruction conducted through online platforms.
vocab.example: Journalists, scientists and public figures increasingly face networked harassment designed to silence them.

vocab.definition: The gradual weakening of shared facts, mutual trust and institutional legitimacy caused by toxic online dynamics.
vocab.example: Democratic corrosion is visible in declining trust metrics and rising belief in baseless conspiracies.

idioms.definition: To maintain firm protective standards against pressure to weaken them.
examples: Regulators must hold the line on platform accountability despite intense lobbying.
Once major platforms secure permanent immunity, it becomes harder to hold the line anywhere.
Democratic societies need to hold the line on the basic integrity of their information environment.

arguments.claim: Engagement-maximising algorithms systematically amplify false, extreme and emotionally charged content at the expense of accuracy and social cohesion.
arguments.explanation: Platform ranking systems are optimised to maximise time spent and interactions. Content that triggers anger, fear or tribal identity reliably outperforms nuanced or corrective material. Internal research from major companies and independent studies have both documented this dynamic. The result is an information environment in which false claims can outrun fact-checks, fringe narratives reach mass audiences, and political polarisation is continuously reinforced. Individual users cannot easily escape the effect because the same incentives shape what they are shown even when they seek balanced sources. When the primary public square is structured this way, democratic discourse is degraded at scale. Regulation that requires transparency of ranking systems, independent auditing of amplification effects, and duties to reduce the spread of demonstrably harmful falsehoods is a necessary corrective. Leaving the architecture of public conversation to engagement metrics alone has already produced measurable damage to shared reality.

arguments.claim: The design of major platforms produces measurable harms to mental health, sleep and attention, especially among children and adolescents.
arguments.explanation: Large-scale observational and experimental studies link heavy social-media use with increased rates of anxiety, depression, body-image distress and sleep disturbance in young people. The mechanisms are well understood: social comparison, fear of missing out, discontinuous reward schedules, and the displacement of offline activity and rest. Platforms have known about these effects for years yet continue to deploy features that maximise session length and emotional intensity. Parents and schools cannot fully counteract systems engineered by teams of behavioural scientists and tested on millions of users. Age-appropriate design duties, default privacy and time limits, restrictions on manipulative features for minors, and independent safety testing are proportionate responses. Treating the current design regime as an untouchable expression of free expression ignores the power imbalance between developing minds and industrial-scale attention extraction.

arguments.claim: Platforms currently enjoy a degree of legal immunity that is unmatched by any other industry that shapes public safety and discourse at comparable scale.
arguments.explanation: In several major jurisdictions, online intermediaries benefit from broad protections against liability for user-generated content. These protections were created when the internet was smaller and more decentralised. They now shield companies that actively curate, rank and amplify content for billions of people. No newspaper, broadcaster or public venue enjoys equivalent freedom from responsibility for the foreseeable consequences of its systems. The result is under-investment in safety, slow responses to coordinated abuse, and persistent distribution of material that would be illegal or heavily restricted in any offline equivalent. Reforming intermediary liability to require reasonable care, rapid response to illegal content, and accountability for algorithmic amplification does not abolish free speech; it ends an anomalous privilege that has allowed systemic harms to continue with limited legal consequence.

arguments.claim: Online disinformation and coordinated influence campaigns have already demonstrably affected elections, public-health compliance and social stability in multiple countries.
arguments.explanation: Documented cases range from foreign interference operations to domestic networks that deliberately spread false claims about voting procedures, vaccines, and public figures. The speed and low cost of digital distribution allow small actors to achieve outsized reach. Once false narratives achieve critical mass they become resistant to correction because of confirmation bias and algorithmic reinforcement. The cumulative effect is reduced trust in electoral processes, lower uptake of public-health measures, and heightened inter-group hostility. Media literacy is necessary but insufficient against industrial-scale, micro-targeted campaigns. Platform obligations to detect and limit coordinated inauthentic behaviour, label manipulated media, and provide researchers with data access are practical tools that have already shown partial effectiveness where implemented. Continuing to treat these operations as an unavoidable cost of an open internet underestimates their capacity to degrade democratic capacity.

arguments.claim: The concentration of power over public discourse in a handful of private companies is itself a democratic risk that requires structural response.
arguments.explanation: A small number of platforms now intermediate the majority of online political conversation, news consumption and social coordination in many countries. Their content policies, ranking decisions and enforcement practices therefore function as de-facto public rules. These companies are accountable primarily to shareholders and advertisers, not to citizens. When their decisions affect election integrity, public health or the visibility of entire viewpoints, the absence of democratic oversight becomes a structural problem. Regulation that mandates transparency, due-process standards for content decisions, interoperability, and independent oversight does not nationalise speech; it subjects a critical public infrastructure to basic standards of accountability. Leaving decisions of this magnitude solely to private corporate governance is incompatible with the principle that the rules of public discourse should ultimately answer to the public.

arguments.claim: Children are uniquely vulnerable to online exploitation, addictive design and harmful content, yet current protections remain fragmented and easily circumvented.
arguments.explanation: Young users encounter sexual content, self-harm material, extreme challenges, predatory contact and commercial manipulation at rates that would be unacceptable in any physical environment designed for children. Age verification is weak, parental tools are incomplete, and recommendation systems can rapidly escalate exposure. The commercial incentive is to maximise engagement across all age groups, including those still developing impulse control and critical evaluation skills. Stronger age-assurance requirements, default child-safe modes, bans on targeted advertising to minors, and duties to prevent known harmful recommendation pathways are already being adopted or proposed in several jurisdictions. These measures recognise that the open internet, left to market forces alone, systematically under-protects the young. Childhood is not a temporary market segment; it is a developmental stage that societies have always surrounded with special safeguards.

arguments.claim: Networked harassment and pile-on dynamics silence legitimate voices and shrink the range of people willing to participate in public life.
arguments.explanation: Coordinated abuse campaigns can subject individuals to thousands of threats, doxxing attempts and reputational attacks within hours. Women, minorities, journalists, scientists and local officials are frequent targets. Many reduce their online presence or exit public discussion altogether. The result is a chilling effect that disproportionately removes moderate and evidence-based voices while rewarding those willing to operate in toxic environments. Platform enforcement is often slow, inconsistent or easily gamed. Clearer legal pathways for victims, faster removal obligations for credible threats, and design changes that reduce the velocity of pile-ons are required. Free expression is not protected by systems that make participation in democratic debate contingent on enduring industrial-scale abuse. Safety from targeted harassment is a precondition for a genuinely open public sphere.

arguments.claim: The economic model of surveillance advertising creates systemic incentives to maximise data extraction and behavioural influence at the expense of user autonomy.
arguments.explanation: Most major consumer platforms derive revenue from increasingly precise prediction and targeting of human behaviour. This model rewards the collection of ever more intimate data and the refinement of techniques that shape attention, emotion and choice. Users cannot meaningfully negotiate the terms; the alternative is often exclusion from essential social and informational services. The long-term effect is an asymmetry of power in which a few companies possess detailed behavioural maps of entire populations while individuals operate with minimal insight or control. Stronger data-minimisation requirements, purpose limitation, bans on certain forms of sensitive inference, and rights to genuine service alternatives without surveillance are necessary to restore a measure of autonomy. An information society organised primarily around behavioural extraction is incompatible with the dignity and self-determination that democratic cultures claim to value.

arguments.claim: Self-regulation and media literacy have been tried for years and have demonstrably failed to contain the scale of current harms.
arguments.explanation: Platforms have issued successive policy updates, transparency reports and partnerships with fact-checkers. Governments have funded digital-literacy programmes. Civil-society organisations have developed tools and campaigns. Despite these efforts, measures of polarisation, youth mental-health distress, belief in false narratives, and online abuse have continued to rise or remain stubbornly high in many societies. The gap between voluntary measures and outcomes indicates that the underlying incentives and architectural features are stronger than goodwill or education alone. When a system is designed to maximise engagement and the most engaging material is often the most harmful, appeals to individual responsibility cannot compensate for structural drivers. Regulatory intervention that changes incentives and design defaults is therefore not a rejection of personal agency; it is a recognition that agency operates inside architectures that currently work against it.

arguments.claim: Other high-impact industries accept safety regulation, product liability and design standards; treating the internet as uniquely exempt is no longer justified by its scale or consequences.
arguments.explanation: Automobiles, pharmaceuticals, food, aviation and financial services all operate under detailed safety regimes because their failures impose large social costs. The internet now mediates elections, public health behaviour, mental health, commerce and social coordination at a scale that rivals or exceeds these sectors. The original rationale for extreme regulatory forbearance — a young, fragile medium that needed space to grow — no longer applies to dominant platforms that shape the daily experience of billions. Applying proportionate duties of care, safety testing for algorithmic systems, and accountability for foreseeable harms simply extends to the digital domain principles long accepted offline. The claim that any such extension inevitably becomes authoritarian censorship confuses the existence of rules with the absence of freedom. Well-designed regulation can protect both open expression and the basic conditions that make democratic discourse possible.

vocab.definition: The gradual expansion of content controls beyond their original justification into broader suppression of disfavoured views.

vocab.definition: The delay, cost and uncertainty that heavy regulation imposes on new services, features and competitors.

vocab.definition: The capacity of individuals to choose platforms, curate their experience, and develop critical skills rather than remaining passive recipients.
vocab.example: Tools for filtering, blocking and media literacy enhance user agency more sustainably than top-down controls.

vocab.definition: The splitting of the global internet into incompatible national regimes that raise costs and reduce interoperability.

vocab.definition: The reduction in legitimate expression caused by fear of legal, platform or social punishment.

vocab.definition: The ability of a network to continue functioning and evolving because no single point of control can shut it down or dictate its development.
vocab.example: The internet’s decentralised resilience has allowed it to survive technical failures and political pressure.

vocab.definition: Regulation that targets specific, demonstrated harms with narrowly tailored tools rather than broad architectural mandates.
vocab.example: Proportional governance focuses on illegal content and clear deception rather than redesigning the entire medium.

arguments.claim: The open internet has produced extraordinary gains in knowledge access, economic opportunity, social connection and political accountability that dwarf the harms attributed to it.
arguments.explanation: Billions of people now have immediate access to educational material, scientific research, market information and diverse cultural expression that were previously restricted by geography, cost or gatekeepers. Small businesses reach global customers; dissidents document abuses; patients find medical information; families separated by migration stay connected. These gains are not marginal; they represent a structural expansion of human capability. Harms such as misinformation, addiction and abuse are real and require response, yet they must be weighed against this background of large-scale benefit. Regulatory regimes that significantly raise the cost of publishing, hosting or innovating risk reducing the very openness that generated the gains. Proportionate responses target specific illegal or clearly harmful behaviours without redesigning the medium into a permissioned system. The net social value of an open architecture remains strongly positive.

arguments.claim: Most serious online harms are already illegal; the primary failure is enforcement and cross-border cooperation, not the absence of new speech-restrictive rules.
arguments.explanation: Fraud, incitement to violence, child sexual abuse material, credible threats and many forms of harassment are criminal offences in most jurisdictions whether they occur online or offline. The difficulty lies in detection, attribution, jurisdictional cooperation and the speed of digital distribution. Creating broad new categories of restricted lawful speech does not solve these operational problems and introduces new ones. Resources directed at better investigative capacity, faster international mutual legal assistance, and specialised platform reporting channels for clearly illegal content address the actual bottleneck. Expanding the scope of prohibited expression, by contrast, multiplies the volume of content that must be assessed, increases the risk of error and over-removal, and invites political pressure to suppress disfavoured but legal views. Effective policy distinguishes sharply between illegal content and lawful content that some find harmful.

arguments.claim: Heavy platform liability for user-generated content creates strong incentives for over-removal and the silencing of controversial but legitimate speech.
arguments.explanation: When intermediaries face significant legal risk for material posted by users, the rational response is to remove first and ask questions later. Automated filters and risk-averse moderation teams err on the side of deletion, especially for content that is politically or culturally contested. Independent studies of content-moderation systems already document high rates of false positives affecting news reporting, satire, minority languages and legitimate political debate. Broadening liability would intensify this dynamic. Smaller platforms and non-commercial hosts, unable to afford large trust-and-safety teams, would become particularly cautious or exit the market, further concentrating power in the largest firms. The resulting environment is less open, less diverse and more hospitable to whichever viewpoints the dominant moderators or the most aggressive complainants prefer. Preserving robust intermediary protections for lawful speech, while requiring rapid action against clearly illegal material, remains the better balance.

arguments.claim: Centralised regulatory control over online speech creates a permanent infrastructure for political abuse that future governments will be tempted to exploit.
arguments.explanation: Rules created with benign intentions to reduce misinformation or hate speech supply the legal and technical tools for later, less benign uses. Once platforms are required to police broad categories of harmful content, the definition of harm becomes a political prize. Governments of every orientation have already pressured platforms to remove lawful criticism, suppress inconvenient reporting, or amplify preferred narratives. Expanding the formal regulatory mandate increases both the capacity and the perceived legitimacy of such pressure. Democracies are not immune; the same mechanisms can be turned against opposition voices, scientific dissent or minority communities when political winds shift. Architectural and liability rules that keep the cost of suppression high, and that leave ultimate judgments about lawful speech to courts rather than to administrative or corporate bureaucracies, are safeguards against this predictable dynamic. Safety regulation that ignores the abuse potential of its own instruments is incomplete.

arguments.claim: Users retain significant agency through choice of platforms, filtering tools, social norms and critical skills; treating them as passive victims understates both capacity and responsibility.
arguments.explanation: Individuals can select services with different moderation philosophies, install blockers and filters, curate feeds, and develop habits of verification. Parents and schools can teach evaluation skills and set boundaries. Civil-society organisations produce rating systems, media-literacy curricula and counter-speech. These mechanisms are imperfect and unevenly distributed, yet they are real and improvable. Policy that begins from the premise of widespread helplessness tends toward comprehensive architectural mandates that reduce choice and experimentation. Empowerment strategies — better default tools, stronger data portability, support for alternative platforms, and sustained literacy investment — work with user agency rather than replacing it. A free society should prefer approaches that expand the capacity of citizens to navigate the information environment over approaches that permanently place that navigation in the hands of regulators and dominant firms.

arguments.claim: The global and borderless character of the internet means that purely national regulatory regimes produce fragmentation, compliance burdens and reduced utility without fully solving transnational harms.
arguments.explanation: Content hosted in one country is accessible in another. Strict national rules therefore either remain incomplete or require extraterritorial assertions of authority that other states reject. The result is a patchwork of conflicting obligations, geo-blocking, and higher costs for any service that operates across borders. Smaller innovators are disproportionately affected. Users lose seamless access to the global pool of information and services that constitutes much of the internet’s value. Transnational harms such as coordinated disinformation or cross-border exploitation require international cooperation on enforcement and standards, not the multiplication of incompatible national redesigns of the medium. Harmonised, narrowly focused rules on clearly illegal content are more achievable and less damaging than unilateral attempts to reconstruct the global network according to each jurisdiction’s preferred speech norms.

arguments.claim: Innovation in content moderation, user controls and alternative governance models is more likely to emerge from competition and experimentation than from uniform top-down mandates.
arguments.explanation: Different communities have different tolerances and priorities. Some users want maximal openness; others prefer heavily curated environments. Platforms already compete on safety features, transparency tools and community standards. New technical approaches to provenance, reputation systems and decentralised moderation continue to appear. Heavy, uniform regulation risks freezing a single model, raising barriers to entry, and reducing the incentive to develop better voluntary solutions. Historical experience with speech and media technologies shows that the most durable improvements often come from social norms, user tools and market differentiation rather than from comprehensive prior restraint. Regulatory humility that sets outer boundaries against clear illegality while leaving space for diverse approaches is more compatible with continued progress than the attempt to engineer a single optimal information environment from the centre.

arguments.claim: Many measured harms attributed to the internet have complex causes; attributing them primarily to platform design risks misdirected and ineffective policy.
arguments.explanation: Trends in polarisation, youth mental health, loneliness and declining trust predate or run parallel to the rise of particular platforms and have been influenced by economic insecurity, demographic change, media fragmentation and institutional performance. Experimental and quasi-experimental studies of social-media effects show mixed and often modest average impacts once confounding factors are considered. Policy that treats engagement algorithms as the master variable therefore risks both over-estimating the leverage of design changes and under-investing in deeper social and economic drivers. This does not mean design is irrelevant; it means that claims of large causal effects require strong evidence and that regulatory interventions should be evaluated for actual outcome improvement rather than for symbolic toughness. A proportionate response remains focused on the most clearly demonstrated and severe harms rather than on a general reconstruction of online life.

arguments.claim: Existing legal tools — defamation, fraud, incitement, child-protection statutes, data-protection law and consumer protection — already supply a substantial framework that can be modernised without rewriting the basic architecture of the internet.
arguments.explanation: Courts and regulators have adapted older doctrines to digital contexts for decades. Targeted updates to these bodies of law can address non-consensual intimate images, certain forms of coordinated inauthentic behaviour, and clear gaps in child protection without imposing general duties to police lawful speech. Data-protection regimes already constrain certain forms of surveillance advertising and can be strengthened. Consumer-protection principles can require clearer disclosure of ranking and targeting practices. These incremental, legally grounded approaches build on established concepts of harm and responsibility. They avoid the open-ended discretion and definitional battles that accompany broad new categories such as “harmful but legal” content. Strengthening and properly resourcing the enforcement of existing norms is often more effective and less dangerous to openness than the creation of expansive new regulatory regimes.

arguments.claim: A free society accepts a higher level of discursive risk as the price of an open public sphere; the alternative is a managed information environment whose long-term costs to liberty and discovery are severe.
arguments.explanation: Every expansion of communication technology — printing, post, telegraph, radio, television — generated moral panics and calls for control. In each case societies that preserved relatively open architectures ultimately captured larger gains in knowledge, accountability and cultural vitality. The internet intensifies both the benefits and the pathologies of open communication. The choice is not between a perfectly safe managed system and a perfectly chaotic open one; it is between a system that retains high generative capacity at the cost of ongoing moderation challenges, and a system that reduces those challenges by permanently lowering the ceiling on spontaneous publication and association. Liberal societies have historically judged that the first option, constrained by targeted rules against force and fraud, is preferable. That judgment remains sound. The task is to improve the tools and norms that help citizens navigate openness, not to abandon openness as the foundational principle of the medium.
